title: Ang 1105–1106: Namdev, Jaidev, Ravidas
tomorrow: what does courage feel like in your hands?

cards: Gym class, picking teams. The kid who always gets chosen last is suddenly named captain, and the whole room goes quiet. Who did that?

Ravidas asks a question like that on ang 1106, about himself. He was born into a family people of his time refused to touch, and he writes: who but You would put a royal canopy over my head? So here's today's argument.
Is that canopy about how people treat each other, or about the soul?

teach.b: These final pages of Maru hold short hymns by three Bhagats: Namdev, Jaidev and Ravidas. Ravidas's hymn, in paraphrase: O Beloved, who but You could do such a thing?
Cherisher of the poor, You set a royal canopy over my head. The one whose touch the world thought polluting, on him You poured mercy. My Lord raises the low up high, and fears no one.
Then he names others who crossed over, Namdev, Kabir, Trilochan, Sadhna, Sain. Now, two readings, both held by thoughtful Sikhs. The first says: this is about the world.
Ravidas names his own shunned birth, out loud, in scripture. The Gurus then put his words in the Granth, and built a community where everyone eats seated together in langar.
The canopy is dignity, here, among real people. The second says: this is about the soul.

The canopy isn't social rank; it's honor before God, and before God, worldly rank never mattered in either direction. Push on rank too hard and you've made it important again. Each side has a strong case.
The first keeps the hymn from floating away into the clouds. The second keeps it from shrinking into only a social program. Either way, the hymn's question stands.

how: The Maru hymns of Namdev, Jaidev and Ravidas are sung in kirtan and read in order in a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Ravidas's 'aisee laal tujh bin kaun karai' is a well-known kirtan hymn.

games.q: who but You — tap the pairs.
p: a royal canopy over my head

s: Ravidas hides where he came from in his hymn
he names it: the one whose touch the world thought polluting, raised up.
in this hymn Ravidas names Namdev, Kabir, Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain as ones who crossed over
the Bhagats together, all raised by the same One.
Sikhs read this hymn only as social teaching, never spiritual
some stress dignity among people, some honor before God; some hold both.

games.q: you read Ravidas's canopy as honor before God. your friend says it's about real dignity in the world. what's the strongest case for her side?
o: he names his shunned birth, and the Gurus seated everyone together in langar.
the hymn never mentions God at all, so it can only be social.
social readings are newer, so they must be more accurate.
games.why: her best case is in the text and the community: Ravidas names his birth, and the langar seats all together. yours: before God rank never mattered.

practice: Let your head bow forward a little, chin toward your chest, the way you might feel when you've been overlooked.
Then, slowly, over a few breaths, lift it until you're looking straight ahead, as if something were being held over you. Stay there, level, for the rest of the sit.

carryVoice: Keep this: who but you, raising the one the world looked down on. Day fifteen-seventy-eight, head level.
